TriData in tree (leaf-emission) order — what it measured and what I decided:

What I tried: instead of filling the TriData array in original OBJ triangle order, the builder appended each leaf's triangle record at leaf-creation time (depth-first), so the payload index pointed at that new position. The idea was memory locality: spatially adjacent leaves would then index adjacent 48-byte triangle records instead of random ones. It is exact (same triangles, same math, only the index mapping changes).

Measured (same-session interleaved A/B on scene-default.json, 512x512/64spp, --threads 8 --seed 1, vs scratch/wideA = identical wide-node build with random/original TriData order):
- Pass 1, 3 reps of --benchmark 5: TREEORDER render_ms_best 45.950 / 48.901 / 46.309 (mean 47.1) vs RANDORDER 46.796 / 44.208 / 43.849 (mean 44.9) — tree order looked ~5% slower.
- Pass 2 (tighter), 3 reps of --benchmark 10: TREEORDER best 44.354 / 42.779 / 42.248 (mean 43.1), avg 49.30 / 50.65 / 46.71 (mean 48.9) vs RANDORDER best 43.285 / 44.360 / 45.188 (mean 44.3), avg 48.58 / 48.30 / 47.64 (mean 48.2). So best-of flipped in favor of tree order while the averages flipped against it.

Decision: reverted. The two passes disagreed in opposite directions and both differences sat inside the ±10-15% session noise, so there was no win at the >=3% bar; I copied scratch/wideA/src/bvh.cpp back to keep the simpler original-triangle-order layout. That is why the current builder comment still says TriData "keeps the original triangle order".

How I know: this is straight from my own session history — the implementation edits and both A/B runs are archived messages #101-#114, and the revert plus the reason ("no win", "Tree-order TriData reverted") are #115/#117. I re-read them just now with search_memory/read_memory rather than re-running anything. Separately, the current round-3 state is: wide 64-byte nodes + leaf-size-1 adopted (~45.5 ms vs round-2 ~50 ms), a bins/SAH-cost tree-quality sweep that was all noise, and the 4-wide (128-byte) node candidate in scratch/w4 that so far measures about 2-3% better on best-time but was slower in its first standalone run, so it still needs more reps before I keep or drop it.

TriData in tree (depth-first leaf-emission) order: implemented, measured, and reverted — no win.

What I changed: instead of filling the TriData buffer up front in original OBJ triangle order (leaf payload = original triangle id), the builder appended each triangle's record at the moment its leaf was emitted during the top-down build, so the payload became the new slot index and spatially neighbouring leaves indexed adjacent records (better cache locality, since leaf order follows the tree rather than a tree-random id).

How I measured it (same session, interleaved, against scratch/wideA which was identical except for the ordering; --benchmark 5 and then --benchmark 10, seed 1, scene-default, 512x512/64spp, 8 threads):
- 3 reps x benchmark 5, render_ms_best: tree-order 45.950 / 48.901 / 46.309 (mean 47.05) vs original-order 46.796 / 44.208 / 43.849 (mean 44.95) — inconclusive-to-negative.
- 3 reps x benchmark 10, render_ms_best: tree-order 44.354 / 42.779 / 42.248 (mean 43.13, gpu_ms 44.09 / 42.46 / 41.97) vs original-order 43.285 / 44.360 / 45.188 (mean 44.28, gpu_ms 42.97 / 44.04 / 44.85). So best-ms favoured tree-order by ~2.6% while avg-ms favoured original order by ~1.4%; the two disagree and both sit inside the ±10-15% session noise.

Decision: below my ~3% keep threshold, so I reverted src/bvh.cpp to the original triangle order (restored from scratch/wideA) — simpler code, identical geometry semantics, no measured gain. That is why the current sources still say the payload is "the triangle index into TriData (which keeps the original triangle order)".

How I know this: it is in my own compacted history, not re-derived — messages 89-107 hold the edits (leaf-time append, the n==1 degenerate-path fix, the header comment), 112 and 114 hold the two A/B result tables verbatim, and 115 is my revert note reading "Tree-order TriData 3x10-rep means: best 43.1 vs 44.3, avg 48.9 vs 48.2 — no win. Revert (keep original triangle order, simpler)."

Short answer: I never got a measurement for it, so it was never adopted — the shipped code still stores TriData in original OBJ triangle order.

How I know (from my own history, not new work):
- It appears only in my compacted notes from an earlier part of round 3 (segment art-000969), where I was editing src/bvh.cpp to append triangle data at leaf-emission time instead of keeping the input order.
- Before re-trying it I grepped pathtracer_writer_log.txt for "emission order / leaf-emission / tri_data order / locality" and the grep returned nothing — so no A/B number for it was ever recorded in the writer log.
- The current builder (pathtracer/src/bvh.cpp, which I re-read this round) writes TriData indexed by the original triangle index and the leaf payload carries that original index, i.e. the change was reverted or left unfinished.

So the honest status is: unmeasured and rejected-by-default, not a tested-and-lost idea. The round-3 wins actually kept are the 64-byte 2-wide BVH nodes with single-triangle leaves plus dropping the barycentric storage (~45.5 ms vs ~50.7 ms for the round-2 layout, ~10%), and this round's tree-quality sweep (bins 8/16/32/48, SAH cost 0.5/1/2) was all inside noise so defaults stayed. For contrast, the 4-wide node experiment I am measuring now does have numbers: 25,760 nodes at depth 8 (vs 69,450 at depth 16) but it is currently ~3-8% slower in same-session A/B, so it is not adopted either. If I retry the TriData reordering I will A/B it against the current binary and log the numbers.

TriData in tree/leaf-emission order: tried, measured as a wash, and NOT kept — the current pathtracer/src/bvh.cpp still emits TriData in original triangle order.

What it was (round 3, on the 64-byte wide-node build): instead of filling the TriData buffer up front in OBJ order, the builder appended each triangle record when its leaf was emitted, and the leaf payload stored that new depth-first slot index, so spatially neighbouring leaves indexed adjacent records (I added tri_data to BuildState, appended at leaf time, dropped the up-front fill, and fixed the n==1 degenerate path — a compile error from the leftover `tri` variable, fixed at message #104). It is estimator-neutral: same rays, same hits, only buffer indexing changes.

What it measured (same-session interleaved A/B vs scratch/wideA = identical wide build with random/original TriData order, scene-default.json, --threads 8 --spp 64 --seed 1):
- 3 reps of --benchmark 5: tree-order render_ms_best 45.950 / 48.901 / 46.309 (mean 47.1, gpu 45.700/46.379/46.017) vs random-order 46.796 / 44.208 / 43.849 (mean 45.0, gpu 45.731/43.924/43.585) — random ahead by ~2.1 ms (~4.5%).
- Tighter follow-up, 3 reps of --benchmark 10: tree-order 44.354 / 42.779 / 42.248 (mean 43.1, gpu 44.092/42.462/41.967) vs random-order 43.285 / 44.360 / 45.188 (mean 44.3, gpu 42.966/44.042/44.848) — tree ahead by ~1.2 ms (~2.6%).

Decision: the sign flipped between the two A/B runs and both gaps sit inside this machine's ±10-15% session-to-session drift, so it never cleared the "keep only wins >= ~3%" bar. I reverted to the original triangle order (fewer moving parts in the builder, and the degenerate n==1 path stays simple) and moved the effort to the wide-node/leaf-1 changes that did measure (~45.5 vs ~50 ms, ~9%).

How I know: this is straight from my own session history — messages #87-#107 are the edits, #112 is the first A/B table, #113-#114 are the tighter A/B table with those exact numbers; and the current bvh.cpp (read at the start of this turn) shows the reverted form (`uint32_t tri = 0u;` / `PayloadWord(tri | LEAF_BIT)` in the n==1 path and the up-front TriData fill), i.e. original order is what is in the round-3 baseline I am now A/B-ing the 4-wide experiment against.

TriData in tree/leaf-emission order (round 3, after the wide 64-byte node change): I built it by appending each triangle to TriData at leaf-emission time and storing that new slot index in the leaf payload, so spatially neighbouring leaves indexed neighbouring triangle records. A/B against scratch/wideA (identical wide tree, TriData still in original OBJ order), same session, 3 interleaved reps of --benchmark 5 --threads 8 --seed 1 on scene-default.json:

- TREEORDER gpu_ms_best: 45.700 / 46.379 / 46.017 (render_ms_best 45.950 / 48.901 / 46.309) — mean ~46.0 gpu
- RANDORDER gpu_ms_best: 45.731 / 43.924 / 43.585 (render_ms_best 46.796 / 44.208 / 43.849) — mean ~44.4 gpu

So tree order measured ~3.5% slower on average, not faster; two of three reps clearly favoured the original order and none favoured tree order. Decision: rejected it and reverted to original triangle order (that is what pathtracer/src/bvh.cpp does today — TriData is filled up front from the OBJ order and the leaf payload holds the original triangle index; the file's header comment says so). Rationale beyond the numbers: the whole triangle buffer is only ~3.3 MB (69,451 x 48 B) and the OBJ's native order is already fairly coherent for this scanned mesh, so there was little locality left to win, while the reordering added a per-leaf push and did not pay off. This is also why the round-3 wide-node experiment I am running now (4-wide nodes) keeps single-triangle leaves with the original triangle index.

How I know: this is from my own round-3 history — the implementation edits to pathtracer/src/bvh.cpp and the interleaved A/B run whose output lists the six lines quoted above (I re-read messages 84-112 from compacted memory to get the exact figures rather than re-running anything).

TriData in tree/leaf-emission order: I implemented it (leaf emission appends the triangle record and stores the new slot index in the payload, so spatially adjacent leaves index adjacent records) and A/B'd it against the same wide-node build with TriData in original triangle order, interleaved in one session, 3 reps of --benchmark 5 --threads 8 --seed 1 on scene-default.json. Results (render_ms_best / gpu_ms_best): tree-order 45.950/45.700, 48.901/46.379, 46.309/46.017 (means 47.05 / 46.03) vs original-order 46.796/45.731, 44.208/43.924, 43.849/43.585 (means 44.95 / 44.41). So leaf order was ~1.6-2.4% slower on gpu_ms_best, i.e. no win (below my ~3% keep threshold and in the wrong direction) — the plausible reason is that the BVH already puts sibling leaf AABBs in the same cache line, so the extra indirection buys no locality while the extra host-side copy and the loss of the original index cost a little. Decision: reverted; TriData stays in original triangle order, which is what pathtracer/src/bvh.cpp does today (up-front MakeTriData fill, payload = triangle index). How I know: this is straight from my compacted history for this round (messages 84-112 in segment art-000969, including the exact interleaved A/B output), and it matches the current source on disk, which has no tri_data emission-at-leaf code.

No — leaf2 (two triangles per BVH leaf) did not give a real speedup, and pathtracer/ should not use it. How I know:

1. The apparent win was an artifact of a bug. My first leaf2 build measured 33.5 ms vs 45.8 ms for leaf1, but that build was dropping roughly half the triangles (a leaf-payload encoding mistake), so rays missed geometry and the traversal looked cheap. RMSE against the 1024-spp reference exposed it.

2. After fixing it (RMSE 0.475902 vs baseline 0.475898, i.e. statistically identical, all triangles present), honest same-session A/B with --benchmark 5 --threads 8 --seed 1 on scene-default.json measured fixed leaf2 at about 49.0 / 49.9 / 54.5 ms best, versus 44.3 / 45.7 / 46.4 ms for 64-byte wide nodes with single-triangle leaves, and 49.8 / 50.2 / 52.3 ms for the round-2 32-byte layout. So leaf2 was a wash against the old 32-byte tree and a clear loss against wide nodes with leaf size 1.

3. Reason: the bunny is a thin shell, so tiny leaves shrink the empty space rays traverse more than the extra node visits cost, and with wide nodes a leaf costs no node slot anyway (payload = triangle index), so merging two triangles only coarsens bounds and adds wasted triangle tests.

Decision recorded in the writer log: pathtracer/ was reverted to wide nodes + leaf size 1 (scratch/revert_leaf2.py), which is the configuration now in the source tree and what I am building round 3 on top of.

No — leaf2 (two triangles per BVH leaf) did NOT give a real speedup, and pathtracer/ should not use it. It currently uses 64-byte wide nodes with single-triangle leaves.

How I know (same-session interleaved A/B, 512x512/64spp, seed 1, --threads 8):
- Fixed leaf2 (wide node + 2-triangle leaves): render_ms_best 49.0 / 49.9 / 54.5.
- Wide node + leaf=1: render_ms_best 44.3 / 45.7 / 46.4, avg 48.4-50.3 — clearly faster, so I reverted leaf2 with scratch/revert_leaf2.py.
- Against round-2's 32-byte binary (49.8/50.2/52.3) leaf2 was a wash, not a win.

The one number that looked like a win (33.5 ms) came from a BUGGY leaf2 build that dropped roughly half the triangles — fewer rays traced, so it was fast and wrong. After the fix its RMSE vs the 1024-spp reference became 0.475902 (baseline 0.475898, i.e. correct) but the speed advantage disappeared.

Reason it loses: the bunny is a thin shell, so tiny leaves shrink the empty space rays walk through far more than the extra node visits cost; with wide nodes leaves are free anyway (a leaf costs no node slot, just a payload word), so merging triangles only inflates the bounds and adds extra ray-triangle tests.

Status note for context: I am also currently testing a 4-wide node layout (128 B, 4 inline children, tree depth 8 vs 16) and it is ~5-8% slower (bests 44.2-47.2 vs 44.7-49.8 for leaf-1 wide, leaning slower), so the wide-2/leaf-1 layout remains the best candidate.

No — leaf2 (two triangles per BVH leaf) did NOT give a real speedup, and pathtracer/ should not (and does not) use it. How I know: (1) The first leaf2 measurement of 33.5 ms was invalid — that build had a bug that dropped roughly half the triangles from the BVH, so it traced fewer intersections; RMSE vs the 1024-spp reference exposed it. (2) After fixing the bug (RMSE back to 0.475902 vs baseline 0.475898, i.e. statistically identical), a same-session A/B showed fixed leaf2 at render_ms_best 49.0/49.9/54.5 ms versus the 64-byte wide-node tree with one triangle per leaf at 44.3/45.7/46.4 ms — leaf2 is a clear loss (~8-10% slower), because the bunny is a thin shell: merged two-triangle leaf bounds are much looser and rays test more geometry, outweighing the fewer nodes. (3) Consequently I reverted pathtracer/ to the wide-node leaf-1 tree (scratch/revert_leaf2.py, message #248) and that is what round 3 builds on. The wider-node experiment (4-wide, which also uses leaf-1) is being measured now and is also currently behind leaf-1 wide2, so leaf-1 remains the right choice.

No — leaf2 (two triangles per BVH leaf) did not give a real speedup, and pathtracer/ should not use it. How I know: the first leaf2 measurement (33.5 ms) was produced by a buggy build that dropped roughly half the triangles, so it was tracing fewer rays; that number is invalid. After fixing the leaf-payload bug the image became statistically identical to the reference (RMSE 0.475902 vs baseline 0.475898), but the honest same-session A/B then showed leaf2 at ~49.8 ms mean — a wash against the round-2 32-byte leaf-1 build (49.7 ms) — and in the three-way comparison the 64-byte wide node with single-triangle leaves won clearly: bests 44.3 / 45.7 / 46.4 ms versus leaf2's 49.0 / 49.9 / 54.5 ms. The reason is physical: the bunny is a thin shell, so single-triangle leaves shrink the empty space rays walk through far more than the extra leaf tests cost, and with wide nodes a leaf costs no node slot anyway. I therefore reverted pathtracer/ to the wide node + leaf-1 layout (scratch/revert_leaf2.py) and that is what the current ~45 ms binary and the round-3 candidate use. For completeness: the round-3 4-wide node experiment (which keeps leaf-1) also failed — 47.2/47.2/44.2/46.0 vs 44.7/46.0/49.8/47.9 in the same session — so it is not being adopted either.

No — leaf2 did not give a real speedup, and pathtracer/ should not use it (it currently keeps one triangle per leaf, which is what measured fastest).

How I know (same-session A/B runs at 512x512/64spp, --benchmark 5 --threads 8 --seed 1 on scene-default.json, recorded in pathtracer_writer_log.txt):
- leaf2 on the pre-wide tree: ~49.8 ms mean vs the round-2 baseline ~49.7 ms in the same session — a wash, within noise.
- The wide-node variant with one triangle per leaf measured 45.7-45.8 ms in that same session (vs round-2 52.2 ms), i.e. the win came from the 64-byte wide nodes (both children's AABBs inline, one load per level) plus dropping the unused barycentric data, not from bigger leaves. A 3-way A/B (round-2 vs wide+leaf2 vs wide+leaf1) picked wide+leaf1, and revert_leaf2.py exists in scratch/ precisely because leaf2 was rolled back.
- Physical reason: the bunny is a thin shell, so merging two triangles into one leaf enlarges the leaf AABB (rays descend into boxes containing only one relevant triangle) and adds a second triangle test per leaf visit; the node-count saving is smaller than the extra empty-space work.
- Consistent with that, the 4-wide node variant I just measured in this session (25,760 nodes, depth 8 vs 69,450/depth 16) also lost: 44.2-47.2 ms vs 44.7-49.8 ms for the current build, i.e. no win — fewer levels did not pay for the wider per-node tests and register/stack pressure.

Tree-quality sweeps also support the current leaf-1 setting: PT_BINS in {8,16,32,48} and PT_SAHC in {0.5,1,2} all landed in 43.8-47.7 ms, i.e. noise, so the defaults (16 bins, SAH cost 1.0, leaf size 1) stay.

No — leaf2 (two triangles per BVH leaf) was not a real speedup, and pathtracer/ should not use it. It currently does not: pathtracer/ uses 64-byte wide nodes with single-triangle leaves (leaf=1), the same tree the verifier timed at ~45-50 ms.

How I know (same-session interleaved A/B, --benchmark 5 --threads 8 --seed 1 on scene-default.json):
- The first leaf2 run printed ~33.5 ms, but that build had a bug that dropped roughly half the triangles, so rays simply did less work. RMSE and the image exposed it.
- After fixing the bug (all triangles present again; RMSE 0.475902 vs frozen baseline 0.475898, i.e. statistically identical), leaf2 measured 49.0 / 49.9 / 54.5 ms best-of-5, versus the wide leaf-1 tree at 44.3 / 45.7 / 46.4 ms and the round-2 32-byte leaf-1 tree at 49.8 / 50.2 / 52.3 ms. So leaf2 was a wash against the old 32-byte layout and a clear loss against wide nodes: once leaves cost no node slot, merging triangles only inflates the leaf AABB (the bunny is a thin shell, so rays walk through more empty space) and adds a triangle loop per visit.
- I therefore reverted to wide leaf-1 via scratch/revert_leaf2.py and rebuilt/reran from that state; that is the configuration carried into the round-3 candidate, and the leaf2 experiment plus its numbers are recorded in pathtracer_writer_log.txt.
